Biggs said on the floor.

articles.title: Hurricane Lowell leaves trail of destruction across Kauai
articles.summary: Many residents of Kauai are without power and face extensive destruction after Hurricane Lowell lashed the island with rain, flooding and strong winds.
articles.body: POIPU, Hawaii — On Kauai’s south shore, Hurricane Lowell lifted a home off its foundation and split it in two, the storm’s powerful winds thrusting part of the structure across the street. At a nearby Sheraton hotel, the hurricane carried several cars across the parking lot and destroyed the hotel’s oceanfront restaurant. Its pool sits full of sand. These are just two of the many scenes of destruction the hurricane has left in Hawaii after lashing the state’s western islands with heavy rain, widespread flooding and tropical-storm-force winds on Monday and Tuesday. Now the extensive recovery efforts begin. Lowell passed just west of the islands of Niihau and Kauai on Monday as a Category 2 hurricane, prompting the National Weather Service to issue the state’s first-ever tornado watch. Flash flooding was widespread across Kauai, where the NWS recorded preliminary rainfall totals of up to 21 inches. In a video update Wednesday, Kauai County Mayor Derek Kawakami said crews had been dispatched islandwide to assess the aftermath of the storm. “Plan to be without power for a while,” county officials wrote Wednesday on Facebook. “Some areas should expect several days or longer.” Around 80% of homes and businesses remain without power in Kauai County — more than 30,000 customers — according to the tracker poweroutage.us. Gentry Cruz, who manages the property that the storm split in half, was resigned while surveying the extent of the destruction. “It sucks, but I mean, you cannot do nothing about it,” he said. “Mother Nature is Mother Nature.” In Waimea, on Kauai’s southwest coast, Facebook user Benjamin E.J. Apilado shared footage of the destruction in his neighborhood early Tuesday morning, showing fallen coconut trees, downed power lines and an uprooted mango tree that had narrowly missed his car. Other social media users posted videos of destroyed homes, with smashed windows and possessions strewn about. Drone footage captured by photographer Braden Geddes revealed extensive damage to homes and roads across Kauai. Other islands were also battered, including Oahu, where maximum wind gusts topped 50 mph. Parts of the island were inundated with nearly 10 inches of rain, according to preliminary totals from the NWS. One person died on Oahu, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said, though it has not yet been confirmed that the death was storm-related. Lowell has since weakened to a tropical storm and continues to move away from Hawaii, but residual tropical moisture could bring additional precipitation and storms Wednesday over the island chain, which could slow cleanup efforts in some hard-hit areas. This was far from the first storm to leave a trail of damage in Hawaii over the last six months. Parts of Oahu and the Big Island saw intense flooding from Hurricane Lala just weeks ago, with some additional rain from Tropical Storm Moke on the Big Island soon after. In March, more than 25 inches of rain fell over parts of Oahu, with Maui recording more than 19 inches. Lowell was one of three storms in the Pacific Ocean last week. The remnants of Hurricane Marie fueled dangerous surf conditions Tuesday along the coast of Southern California, and leftover tropical moisture is driving up temperatures and humidity across the region this week. A rare extreme heat warning was in effect for Southern California on Wednesday, including for Los Angeles and San Diego. Meanwhile, Hurricane Karina, which had been churning east of the Hawaiian Islands, weakened into a tropical storm on Saturday and did not generate any hazards that affected land. The uptick in storm activity in the Pacific basin is largely being driven by El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterized by warmer-than-usual sea surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific Ocean. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and other forecasting agencies predict an exceptionally strong El Niño, or “super El Niño,” this time around. NOAA last month estimated that this El Niño event has a 69% chance of becoming the strongest on record.

articles.title: Surrogate who refused abortion takes fight to Supreme Court as baby's life hangs in balance
articles.summary: Surrogate McKenna West asks the Supreme Court to block a California ruling that left her unable to advocate for a newborn with a rare heart defect.
articles.body: A surrogate who defied a California couple’s demand to abort their baby after a devastating heart diagnosis is taking her fight to the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing a lower court ruling has left her powerless to advocate for the medically fragile newborn. Attorneys for Alaska cardiac nurse McKenna West filed an emergency application Wednesday, asking Justice Elena Kagan to temporarily block a Los Angeles court ruling that declared the California couple the baby’s legal parents. Kagan handles emergency matters arising from the 9th Circuit, which includes California. She has not ruled on the request. SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION West carried the child under a surrogacy agreement with California couple Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed, who call the baby Rumi. West calls him Gabriel. The baby was born in Texas Aug. 12 with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, or HLHS, a rare condition in which the left side of the heart is severely underdeveloped. KAGAN RECALLS LINDSEY GRAHAM'S VOTE THAT HELPED SEAL HER SUPREME COURT CONFIRMATION The legal war began after the condition was detected during a 20-week ultrasound. West alleges Gilkar and Ahmed asked her to terminate the pregnancy under a provision in their surrogacy agreement covering serious fetal abnormalities. West refused, telling the surrogacy agency she could not abort "this precious baby" after feeling him move and learning treatment was available, according to the filing. She offered to raise the child herself or arrange an adoption if the couple no longer wanted him, while allowing them to walk away from any further financial obligations. Her attorneys allege West was then warned that continuing the pregnancy could expose her to more than $250,000 in financial penalties. CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION Gilkar and Ahmed later turned to a California court to establish their legal rights as the baby’s parents. West argued the case belonged in Alaska under the surrogacy agreement and said she appeared in California solely to challenge the court’s jurisdiction. The Los Angeles Superior Court determined that West had effectively consented to its authority by submitting a 147-page filing that addressed the "substance of the issues," according to the application. West’s lawyers said most of those pages were exhibits supporting her jurisdictional challenge and that she had repeatedly refused to argue the underlying case. "Any reasonable view of consent would recognize that ‘no’ does not mean ‘yes,’" they wrote. West also claims she was never properly served. Her filing says a FedEx package containing the court papers was delivered to her babysitter, who allegedly was not told what was inside. The California court declared Gilkar and Ahmed the baby’s legal parents June 22, and West failed to persuade three state courts to put the ruling on hold. SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION The judge acknowledged during the California proceedings that the dispute "[m]ay be a question of life and death" for the unborn child, according to West’s application. The fight then moved to Texas, where West traveled so the baby could be delivered at a hospital equipped to treat his condition. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secured an emergency order before the birth, directing the hospital to provide life-saving care and preventing the child from being removed from the state. West previously said she had only about one minute with the newborn while his umbilical cord was still attached before he was taken from her. A court order later barred her from seeing or holding him. The baby underwent the first of three anticipated open-heart surgeries Aug. 17. He was later returned to a breathing tube after his condition declined, according to court filings previously reviewed by Fox News Digital. Gilkar said during a hearing last month in Dallas that the couple had remained at their son’s bedside and accused West of trying to take him. "He’s our child," Gilkar said, according to The Associated Press. "He’s the love of our lives." She also told the court the newborn was "suffering a lot" as he struggled to breathe, choked on tubes and required a blood transfusion following surgery, according to the AP. West has said she would abandon her custody effort if a court determined the intended parents were committed to providing the child with life-saving care. But on Sept. 2, a Texas judge upheld the California ruling and removed West from the case. Paxton has also stepped away from the legal fight. HHS WARNS TEXAS HOSPITALS AGAINST DENYING LIFE-SAVING CARE TO NEWBORN WITH DISABILITY West’s attorneys argue she is now barred from receiving information about the baby or defending the order requiring his continued treatment. They allege Gilkar and Ahmed are challenging that medical care order. The couple previously agreed to the baby’s first surgery and said they would approve life-saving care if doctors determined he was a candidate. West is now asking the Supreme Court to temporarily block the California ruling, which could give her a path back into the Texas case. Her attorneys argue the dispute raises a broader constitutional question over whether challenging a court’s authority can itself be treated as accepting that authority. Her lawyers stressed that temporarily blocking the ruling would not decide who the baby’s legal parents are or direct doctors to provide a particular course of treatment. Instead, it could allow West to ask the Texas court to bring her back into the case. Without Supreme Court intervention, her attorneys warned, West will remain shut out of decisions and updates about the baby’s condition as the appeals process plays out. "Unless this Court provides relief from that judgment, M.W. will have no access to information about Baby G.’s condition," West’s attorneys wrote. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP They argued that a victory later could come too late to protect the child. "Relief later in Texas proceedings may only restore her right to protect a child that has already passed," the filing states. Fox News’ Shannon Bream and Bill Mears contributed to this report.

articles.title: ESPN hopes to make Peter Schrager its first homegrown star in over a decade | Bobby Burack
articles.summary: Peter Schrager joins Pat McAfee and Stephen A. Smith as ESPN personalities with shows built around them, but key concerns loom over his path.
articles.body: If you speak to anyone in or around ESPN, they will tell you the same story about Peter Schrager: ESPN wants him to be its next big star. On Thursday, the network will debut "Big Day with Peter Schrager." The program will air weekdays at 2 p.m., as OutKick first reported in July. Schrager joins a short list of individuals with ESPN television shows in 2026 built specifically around their personality. Pat McAfee, Stephen A. Smith, Mike Greenberg and Scott Van Pelt are the others. That group should tell you all you need to know about how the network views Schrager. HERE IS HOW PAT MCAFEE HAS SURPASSED STEPHEN A SMITH AS THE FACE OF ESPN | BOBBY BURACK Schrager will also be the first personality under Burke Magnus’ regime to receive a push toward potential stardom. Remember, ESPN did not make McAfee a star. He was already a star before signing with the network. In fact, ESPN licensed McAfee’s show to a then-record-setting deal because it had so mightily struggled to create new stars in-house. McAfee had leverage because none of the personalities ESPN previously tried to establish had any. That list includes Bomani Jones, Sarah Spain, Katie Nolan, Monica McNutt, Jemele Hill, Michael Smith and Mina Kimes. Schrager represents a change of pace from that group. He fits ESPN’s preferred direction of leaning into the positivity and excitement surrounding sports, rather than the negative and polarizing coverage that had become standard. Last month, ESPN executive Mike Foss emphasized during a town hall the company’s desire to move away from "hot takes." Schrager also provides more expertise than other personalities ESPN hoped to brand around. He has a background in NFL reporting. He is more knowledgeable than those who cover the league primarily through the lens of the culture war. On the surface, Schrager’s prospects are promising. But concerns remain. One involves the executive who hired and elevated him. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Last week, OutKick explained how Magnus undermined his own edict and vision by hiring back Stan Verrett to host a throwaway show on NFL Network. During his first tenure, Verrett represented the very type of behavior Magnus had spent the past few years weeding out, including deranged posts, unprofessional direct messages to reporters, and preposterous race talk. We believe Magnus felt pressure after Ryan Clark name-dropped him in unfounded accusations of racism following Clark’s firing. ESPN did not deny our understanding of Magnus’ position. If Magnus has set out to prove that he is not a racist, he could derail Schrager’s new show by surrounding him with polarizing individuals eager to impress their audiences on Threads, Bluesky, and Black Twitter. This is an issue elsewhere at the company. Nearly every ESPN program features a rotating cast of panelists, most of whom viewers are not tuning in to hear. Get Up is now more about Chris Canty and Chiney Ogwumike than Greenberg, one of the last few difference-makers left at the company. Schrager has not shown that he has the chops to push back against said hysteria. During Super Bowl week, he nodded along on set as NFL defensive lineman Cam Jordan spewed nonsense in an effort to argue that Lamar Jackson is a better postseason quarterback than Josh Allen, despite all evidence to the contrary. That was a bad look for Schrager. He looked scared. WHY DID BURKE MAGNUS HIRE BACK STAN VERRETT? Therefore, the question begs whether Schrager is prepared to push back when, say, McNutt and David Dennis Jr. belittle and downplay Caitlin Clark while further advancing racial narratives. Whether he is could swiftly determine the success and perception of his program. There is a reason NFL Live is growing at double-digit rates while First Take is stagnant. Sports fans want fun, not polarization. We thought Magnus understood that. The hiring of Verrett casts doubt on whether he does. Finally, while live sports and streaming will ultimately define ESPN’s success, it is important that the network casts Schrager right. Most of the company’s biggest stars are around 60 years old, including Stephen A., Greenberg and Van Pelt. At 44, Schrager could have a long runway alongside McAfee, who is 39. Laura Rutledge, 37, Josh Pate, 40, and Malika Andrews, 31, are other potential future stars for the network. If there were ever a sports personality we would strongly advise to stick to sports and stay off X, it would be Peter Schrager. He has the chance and talents to become one of the faces of ESPN for the next decade. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But ESPN hasn't built a star on its own since Stephen A. Smith. That was in 2015. Schrager will have to buck that trend.

articles.title: Autism: Mum cannot understand why son placed on Child Protection Register
articles.summary:
Danielle McQuillan said she does not understand why her son, who has 
autism and severe learning disabilities, was registered.
articles.body:
The mum of a six-year-old boy with autism and severe learning disabilities said she has been left "shaking" and "intimidated" after her son was placed on the Child Protection Register (CPR).

Danielle McQuillan said she does not understand why Zac was registered and says she had been seeking more overnight respite care to help her cope with his complex needs and to spend more time with her daughters.

Zac is non-verbal and his mum said his behaviour can be extremely challenging, including stripping off his clothes and running away when they are out.

The South Eastern Health Trust, who placed him on the register, has been contacted for comment.

The CPR is a register of children who have been identified as being at risk of significant harm.

Eamonn McNally, senior lawyer at the Children's Law Centre, said his organisation is increasingly seeing the CPR used in cases involving children with complex disabilities and additional needs when they are not at risk.

"We have a number of families with significant needs who are under extreme pressure they're at burn out because of a lack of service and support," he said.

"That shouldn't equate to a registration on the child protection register that should equal support being put in place to keep that family together."

When a child is placed on the CPR social workers will typically carry out unannounced visits to witness the family in a regular day-to-day setting.

McQuillan said these visits can be "intimidating" as she does not know why her son has been placed on the register.

"I've been trying to get some overnight respite as I want to be a mum to my girls as well as Zac," she said.

"I had a disagreement with a social worker about getting a break and they said 'we can't parent your child more than we already do'.

"That really hit a nerve with me as someone who works very hard to be a good parent."

McQuillan said the exchange left her feeling "upset and crying".

The next day, she said, two social workers called to her home to inform her that they would be holding a child safeguarding conference with a view to putting Zac on the CPR.

A child safeguarding conference is organised if a child is considered at risk of significant harm.

It usually involves agencies such as social services, medical professionals and schools, meeting with a child's family to share information, identify risks and outline what needs to be done to protect the child, according to the NSPCC .

The conference involved 17 health and education professionals, according to McQuillan, with each asked to vote on whether Zac should be registered.

The decision was taken to place him on the register.

McNally from the Children's Law Centre, was McQuillan's representative at the meeting.

The organisation has called for a review of the process, describing it as "out of date and not fit for purpose".

The NSPCC said the CPR allows relevant agencies, such as emergency responders and schools, to check if a child they are working with is known to be at risk.

McQuillan said being placed on the register has increased her anxiety and stress.

"It has meant the social workers have turned up unannounced at my home," she said.

"I just feel like I'm being watched for a reason that I don't know."

She said on one occasion she took Zac to McDonald's and returned home to find two social workers parked outside.

"I was shaking, I felt so intimidated," she continued.

I think it's because there isn't a proper reason as to why he's been put on it they're almost trying to find a reason now which is why they're turning up."

McNally said families who find themselves on the register can sometimes feel there has been an overreach by social services.

"And what I mean by that is you have people coming into your home checking you out.

"That doesn't actually add anything to the family, in fact it takes away from the time that they have with their child."

articles.title: The one thing you need to do to succeed - according to top bosses
articles.summary: What makes someone stand out in a crowded workplace? Six business leaders tell us what they look for.
articles.body:
What makes someone stand out in a crowded workplace?

For some bosses, it's less about having the perfect CV and more about the way you think, the questions you ask and whether you're prepared to take a chance.

Six business founders and leaders share the qualities they notice most and the advice they would give to people trying to get ahead.

Charlotte Tilbury says one of the biggest things that has driven her career is refusing to let other people set limits on what she can do.

"Nothing is impossible in life - it's only your own limitations you give yourself."

The beauty mogul says there will always be naysayers, and there were plenty of people who told her she was "mad" or that her ideas would not work but it's important to ignore them.

Tilbury recommends trying not to think of setbacks as mistakes, but as opportunities to rethink and improve.

"I don't think about mistakes, I think mistakes are opportunities," she says.

Many of the biggest challenges she faced ultimately made her a stronger business leader and "challenge is opportunity and it leads you to greater places".

Charlie Bowes-Lyon, co-founder of deodorant brand Wild, says attitude matters far more than having the perfect set of skills.

"For me, it's 90% attitude and 10% skills, as skills can be taught, attitude can't."

One thing he wishes he had realised earlier is that even successful people do not always feel as confident as they appear and "everyone is faking it until they're making it".

If you find yourself at a job interview, Bowes-Lyon says it's really important to have a few questions at the end as "candidates who say they have no questions rarely get the job".

One question he recommends asking the interviewer is what success in the job looks like.

Marcia Kilgore, the serial entrepreneur behind brands including Beauty Pie and Soap and Glory, says curiosity is one of the main qualities she looks for when hiring.

She values people who will "roll their sleeves up, ask lots of questions and think about how they can be useful".

Kilgore also says good communication is crucial as she realised early on in her career that a lack of communication is often the reason things break down.

Her advice to communicate well in the workplace is to "listen to what's being asked and take a breath or five" before responding.

"Your response doesn't have to be immediate, but it does have to be considered."

Anabel Kindersley, CEO and co-owner of Neal's Yard Remedies, says one of the best ways to build your skills is to keep saying yes to new opportunities.

"Do everything and say yes to everything - it might feel uncomfortable but do it anyway," she says.

It is an approach that has shaped her own varied career, from working as a child actress to becoming an author and later moving into business.

She adds that honesty really matters and you should be truthful about your experience and confident in what you can offer.

When hiring, Kindersley says she looks for people with "equal EQ as IQ", valuing emotional intelligence alongside ability.

Charlie Nunn, group chief executive of Lloyds Banking Group, says curiosity, resilience and an increasing willingness to think about how AI tools can also be used in the future are some of the skills he values most in his employees.

He also really puts an emphasis on hiring people who are good at working in a team as "at the heart of most jobs is the ability to work together in support of something much bigger".

His advice for building experience is to take on opportunities that are outside your comfort zone.

Nunn says he was "terrified" about taking on retail roles earlier in his career, but found they gave him valuable experience.

"If something feels risky, try and do it as you'll learn more from it and it'll build breadth around your CV that you didn't have previously."

James Reed, chairman and chief executive of recruitment company Reed, says one of the biggest mistakes people make is thinking about what an employer can do for you rather than what you can offer in return.

"The biggest mistake is thinking that the world owes you a living," he says and instead suggests you should ask yourself: "How am I the solution to an employer?"

As AI is increasingly used in recruitment, Reed says applicants need to think about how their skills are being picked up by technology as well as by a person.

"Try and mirror the job description with your skills and experiences in your application," he says, so that the match between what an employer is looking for and what you can offer is clear.

He describes AI as "a wonderful tool", but says it should not replace your own judgement or voice – the aim is for it to strengthen an application rather than expect it to do the work for you.

articles.title: In 2012, an English upland restoration project began fencing sheep out of Tebay Common; 60,000 trees later, lost woodland is returning and 11 new breeding bird species have been recorded since 2016
articles.summary: UK News: An ambitious upland restoration project in Cumbria has turned a once-bare area of sheep-grazed fell into a thriving habitat, bringing back lost native.
articles.body: An ambitious upland restoration project in Cumbria has turned a once-bare area of sheep-grazed fell into a thriving habitat, bringing back lost native woodland and attracting 11 new breeding bird species since 2016. The project at Tebay Common began in 2012 through a partnership between local farmers, landowner Lonsdale Estates, and the Woodland Trust. It was supported by a 10-year government agri-environment scheme. By fencing sheep and semi-feral fell ponies out of 26 hectares of the 128-hectare fell, conservationists allowed 60,000 native trees to grow across the landscape. Research monitoring by South Lakes Ecology and field data collected for the Woodland Trust found that reducing heavy grazing allowed long-dormant seed banks to recover. This has led to what ecologists call "ghost woodlands".Ghost woodlands return to the Cumbrian fellsFor centuries, heavy livestock grazing stopped young trees from growing across the Cumbrian uplands. As a result, the hills lost much of their natural tree cover and understorey plants. "We call these memories 'ghost woodlands'," Peter Leeson, a Woodland Trust representative, told The Guardian in an interview about the project's progress. "Bluebells are popping up and there are patches of bracken, which suggest the soils and seed banks retain the memory of being a woodland despite hundreds of years of sheep grazing." Leeson said planting native trees on a shared common was a major change from traditional land management in the area. "Doing so much tree-planting on a common was groundbreaking," Leeson said. "This was a leap in the dark for the farmers, as much as anyone else. Hats off to them." Documents from Forest Research's national database on natural flood management confirm that the 60,000 trees planted at Tebay Common cover about 12 per cent of the fell. Native species were carefully planted in agreement with local graziers so important livestock gathering routes and open grazing areas could remain.Breeding bird populations show rapid recoveryThe mix of young trees, shrubs and ungrazed plants has quickly changed the area, especially for bird populations. "Birdsong ripples through the valley as first light spills over a ridge line and on to 26 hectares of fenced-off land near Tebay village," reported The Guardian during a visit to the site. "Meadow pipits, reed buntings and stonechats are among the choristers." Ecologist Mike Douglas from South Lakes Ecology has carried out yearly bird surveys across the fenced areas. He found that 11 new breeding bird species had moved into the site since the baseline survey in 2016. By 2024, the restored area had 14 breeding species. "I'm surprised by how quickly birds have colonised, and the diversity of species," Douglas told The Guardian. "We've been conditioned to see the uplands as barren for much of the year. It needn't be that way. We are 10 years into what was ecologically very damaged land." Douglas said more common woodland birds, including blue tits, great tits, dunnocks and blackbirds, are expected to establish breeding territories as the trees grow and the canopy becomes more developed.Practical benefits for flood management and farm incomeThe Tebay Common project has also become an example of how restoration can support natural flood management and rural incomes. A study on nature-based flood solutions by researchers at Lancaster University found that the project combines tree planting with peatland drain blocking and leaky wooden dams. These measures help store more water, improve soil absorption and slow the flow of stormwater into downstream rivers. The financial support behind the project has also helped local hill farming remain viable. The Tebay Common Grazing Association receives £25,600 each year through its environmental agreement to maintain fencing and compensate for lost grazing rights. The money is shared between the landowner and participating farmers. Tim Winder, chairman of the Tebay Common Grazing Association, told The Guardian that environmental schemes are becoming increasingly important for upland livestock farmers as agricultural subsidies change. "We have to look at different ways of farming," Winder said. "We'll invite anyone to work with us." Reports from the Woodland Trust's State of the UK's Woods and Trees publication say that combining targeted woodland creation with existing grazing rights could provide a model for restoring other upland commons across Britain.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iran war looms over Trump at Republican midterm convention in Dallas
articles.summary: Trump supporters say he can rally Republican voters despite concerns over the unpopular war and rising prices.
articles.body:
Dallas, Texas – The Republican midterm convention has represented a gambit for the party: centring US President Donald Trump in the final stretch of the midterm elections, even as the first two years of his second term have cast a polarising political shadow.

That has been particularly true when it comes to the war on Iran, which Trump launched alongside Israel on February 28, and the knock-on effects on affordability in the United States, a key issue for many voters.

As Trump prepared to deliver a keynote address on Wednesday in Dallas, prices for Brent Crude, the global benchmark, rose above $100 a barrel for the first time since July, a reminder of the conflict’s continued fallout for global markets.

Nevertheless, supporters who spoke to Al Jazeera still saw the president as the man to rally Americans to vote Republican in November, as the party fights to hold onto control of the House of Representatives and Senate.

But some voiced concern – or confusion – over the impact of the war.

“This really is a Trump-a-palooza, as people have been saying,” said Carter Eisinger, a 27-year-old electrician who travelled from Fargo, North Dakota.

“I think some people say that in a derogatory way, but I think it’s very much a complimentary phrase,” he added. “The reality of it is we are in a Trump Republican Party.”

Still, Eisinger struggled to see how the war fit into Trump’s “America First” vision.

“In my opinion, I don’t really see the connection of how a war in Iran helps us here in the country,” he said. “If the Iran war is justified, I’m willing to pay the gas prices, but I haven’t seen that justification.”

He felt a similar confusion about the close relationship between the US and Israel.

“At the end of the day, I’m going to come right back to whatever is best for families, young people, anyone in America,” he said. “If it’s helping Israel in a way that helps us, then great… but it needs to help us first.”

Others were more charitable towards Trump’s approach to the Middle East, even if they saw the war on Iran as a misstep.

Bijay Dixit, a 59-year-old photographer from Houston, Texas, gave Trump high marks on his approach to immigration. He also believed Republicans were the party to steward the economy in the years ahead.

But on Iran, he said there had been a “miscalculation”, even if he agreed with the Trump administration’s position that the war was ultimately a necessary response to the totality of Iran’s actions in the 47 years since the Islamic revolution in 1979.

“Iran needed to be stopped at some point,” he said. “When I say miscalculation, what I mean is underestimation of the capacity of the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps].”

Helen Vennett, a 65-year-old small business owner from Maryland and the chairman of her county’s Republican Party, likened the convention to a high-school pep rally.

“All of us need to have cheerleaders in our life… It just gets you fired up again. You kind of need to know that you’re not alone, that there are believers,” she added.

But while she said she broadly supported the Trump administration’s justification for the war, she acknowledged the potential political fallout.

Polls have regularly suggested widespread disapproval among US citizens of the war on Iran, with independents in particular expressing disapproval. Many, in turn, rank affordability as their top issue heading into the midterm vote.

A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll suggested that only a quarter of Americans think the war is worthwhile.

For its part, the Trump administration has downplayed the prospect of ending the war, focusing instead on efforts to open shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz, over which Iran continues to assert its influence.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday as he departed for the convention, Trump sought to temper expectations that the war would end before November’s pivotal vote.

“I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm,” he said, accusing Iran of intentionally holding out until November.

“They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapons,” he said.

He predicted the war would end swiftly after the final votes have been cast.

“They can’t hold out any longer,” he said.

John Russell, 55, from Rockford, Illinois, who regularly travels to Trump rallies as part of the “Front Row Joe’s” group, said he believed voters would still view the first two years of Trump’s second term as a net positive.

“It’s been a small bump with the gas going up,” he told Al Jazeera from the convention.

“But it had to be done. We can’t allow [Iran] to have a nuclear bomb,” he said, referring to one of the administration’s main justifications for the war.

Tehran has long denied seeking a nuclear weapon, with military analysts generally agreeing that destroying its nuclear programme would require a major military escalation, involving boots on the ground.

Russell predicted that the Republican Party’s bet would pay off at the polls.

“It’s going to fire up the base,” he said of the convention. “It’s going to switch some independents to vote for the Trump-backed candidates, and they will win.”

articles.title: Spanish opposition leader calls prime minister a ‘traitor’ over Ceuta migrant crisis
articles.summary: Santiago Abascal branded Pedro Sánchez a "traitor" in parliament over Spain's migrant crisis in the North African enclave of Ceuta amid protests.
articles.body: A Spanish opposition leader branded the country's socialist prime minister a traitor over his government's handling of the influx of migrants in a North African enclave. Santiago Abascal, leader of the Vox party, spoke during a parliamentary session when he asked if Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez was being blackmailed by Morocco amid the border crisis in Ceuta. During his remarks, Abascal called Sánchez a "traitor" and "a dog." FIREBRAND REP UNLOADS ON SOCIALIST PRIME MINISTER AS 'HORDES OF MILITARY AGED MEN' SWARM EUROPEAN COUNTRY Sánchez responded in a heated back-and-forth, saying, "I may be a dog, but I have no master." Abascal then held up sheets of paper one by one that spelled out "Traidor," Spanish for "Traitor." Sánchez then sat down. Spain has seen major protests in response to the migrant arrivals in Ceuta, with critics blaming Sánchez for the crisis and some accusing him of pandering to Morocco. LOCALS TORCH MIGRANT SHELTERS AS SPAIN'S PM POINTS BLAME BEYOND THE BORDER More than 70,000 migrants poured into Ceuta in July. Most of them have returned to Morocco, but many remain in the enclave, with some living in tent encampments on the beach. Meanwhile, Spain’s national intelligence agency issued multiple warnings before the mass crossing of migrants from Morocco into Ceuta in late July, according to declassified documents released by the government on Wednesday, The Associated Press reported. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP On July 29, a day before people began crossing into Ceuta, the National Intelligence Center (CNI) sent an alert via WhatsApp to the Spanish government’s delegation in Ceuta about calls on social media "for an assault on the fence and by sea tomorrow at 8 p.m." "There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers," the declassified WhatsApp message said, "just to give you an idea of its scale." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Illinois mother accused of killing son had intended to poison husband, prosecutors say
articles.summary: People in a group chat with Corie Walsh said her messages before the killing were “out of character,” attorneys said, and the neighbor who found her said she had dilated eyes and a “weird giggle.”
articles.body: The mother accused of killing her young son in a horrifying scene that unfolded inside a suburban Chicago home also made statements about harming her husband, prosecutors said during her first court appearance Tuesday. A wave of new details were revealed before a judge as prosecutors sought to keep Corie Walsh, 40, behind bars pretrial, while her attorneys argued for inpatient medical care, saying the Frankfort mother was suffering from a psychotic episode at the time of her son’s killing. “She was severely mentally ill at the time of incident and requires treatment,” defense attorney Robert Kerr said in court, adding that doctors who treated Walsh following the alleged murder and her attempts of self-harm recommended “immediate” care. Prosecutors argued that Walsh intended to do more than kill her 2-year-old son, Barrett “Bear” Walsh, but also discussed planning to poison her husband. A judge has ordered her detained, saying she poses a risk to her remaining children and husband. New details revealed in court Prosecutors had previously filed documents detailing what they say happened the day Walsh was found in a bloody bathtub and her 2-year-old son dead in her basement, hanging from a rafter. In court Tuesday, they revealed that two other children who live in the home came back from school, saw the situation unfolding and ran to a neighbor for help. The neighbor quickly pulled Barrett down and attempted CPR but said he had no pulse. He was later pronounced dead at an area hospital. The Will County Medical Examiner’s Office ruled his cause of death as asphyxia. An 8-month-old was also in the home at the time and had been left on the floor of an upstairs room unsupervised, prosecutors said. Walsh was ultimately found by the neighbor fully clothed, in a bathtub with bloody water, having injuries to her wrist and thighs, prosecutors said. She told authorities at the time she killed her son because “he was the devil” and “anti Christ,” the court docs showed. She later made statements saying she intended to harm her husband when he arrived home, saying she would “poison him with a drink,” prosecutors said, noting that she also believed she had killed her other children as well. She had drinks at home and a number of prescription bottles, they added. Defense attorneys argued, however, that she was in a state of psychosis when she attempted to take her own life and when she made statements to law enforcement and hospital staff. Friends say they noticed ‘shift’ in Walsh’s texts hours before son’s death Prosecutors, citing witnesses, had previously said Walsh had “recently become very invested in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial,” in which the mother killed her three children before trying to kill herself. The trial generated intense interest for more than a month, deeply dividing the public and drawing attention to issues around maternal mental health after childbirth. Clancy’s attorney said she was suffering from a rare condition called postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors conceded that Clancy had severe mental illness but insisted she was able to understand and control her actions. A judge last week declared a mistrial. According to the court documents, Walsh “had been actively discussing the case via group text message with her friends” up until just hours before the tragic discovery was made inside her home. But on Tuesday, defense attorneys said those witnesses noted some unusual behavior from Walsh hours before the incident unfolded. Members of the group chat described her messages as “confusing” and “out of character.” They said she believed Clancy’s husband killed his children, writing “it was manslaughter, please help I’m really freaking out.” The neighbor who found Walsh also acknowledged she was unlike herself, saying she had dilated eyes and a “weird giggle.” A firefighter and first responder told detectives she was “incoherent” in the ambulance, as well. Defense attorneys noted that Walsh saw a counselor recently and had never previously displayed any signs of abuse toward her children, according to family and friends. Defense attorney calls allegations of a Lindsay Clancy copycat ‘sickening’ Despite similarities and text messages surrounding the Lindsay Clancy case, defense attorneys said mentions of Walsh being a “Lindsay Clancy copycat” are “sickening.” “Describing Corie to a copied Lindsay is to take an easy bait,” Kerr said. Mother was diagnosed with ‘brief psychotic disorder,’ attorney says Kerr said Walsh was “severely mentally ill” at the time of incident and requires treatment. He told a judge she was diagnosed with “brief psychotic disorder.” They argued her mental health was assessed at the hospital, where doctors said she required treatment. Prosecutors argued she would be able to receive treatment while being detained. Funeral held for Barrett Walsh While his mother appeared in court, Barrett was laid to rest Tuesday in a funeral. Walsh’s husband and her mother were not in court, but officials said her husband cooperated with police and social workers. Defense attorneys said the husband and mother “have unwavering love and support” for Walsh. Walsh’s next court appearance is set for Sept. 24. articles.title: Chris Rock says President Trump is correct on one key issue, and it almost redeems his ‘other sins’
articles.summary: Chris Rock says Trump got it right about fake news, calling media bias the one thing that "almost" clears Trump of all his "other sins" in a new interview.
articles.body: Legendary actor and comedian Chris Rock argued that, if nothing else, President Donald Trump is dead-on accurate when criticizing the news as "fake." Rock spoke to Variety about his upcoming film, "Misty Green," offering candid commentary on the entertainment industry. During the interview, Variety noted that Rock still has the same "opinionated, incendiary persona that caught Eddie Murphy’s eye at a New York comedy club one night when Rock was just 19." "Rock was one of the few celebrities to publicly predict Donald Trump would win the 2016 election," Variety wrote. "And speaking about the president today, Rock says, ‘I’m not a fan. But it’s weird when somebody gets one thing right, and the one thing almost clears them of all their other sins. The news is fake. He got that right.’" Curtis Houck, managing editor of the Media Research Center's NewsBusters, responded to Rock's comments in a statement to Fox News Digital. EX-CNN ANCHOR DON LEMON AGREES TRUMP PLAYED LIBERAL NETWORK 'LIKE PUPPETS' "In this day and age, we often find ourselves feeling like we’re approaching cats-and-dogs living together on certain issues, and that includes the acknowledgment that the legacy, elitist media have failed to serve the public," Houck said. "The widespread awareness of both media bias and press ineptitude will be one of President Trump’s longest-lasting legacies. Chris Rock certainly seems to be on the president’s wavelength." In 2023, Rock raised eyebrows by warning U.S. lawmakers that arresting Trump would only make him "more popular." Rock had made the comments while in Washington, D.C., for an event honoring Adam Sandler. He began poking fun at the well-connected crowd, which included former Speaker Nancy Pelosi and members of President Biden's administration. CRAIG FERGUSON REVEALS WHY TRUMP JOKES ARE MISSING FROM HIS NEW COMEDY TOUR "Are you guys really going to arrest Trump?" Rock asked. "Do you know this is only going to make him more popular. It's like arresting Tupac. He's just gonna sell more records. Are you stupid?" Fox News Digital's Anders Hagstrom contributed to this report. articles.title: A journalist is named king of a Ugandan monarchy that just lost its onetime ‘boy king’
articles.summary: A news anchor was unexpectedly named the next monarch of Uganda’s Tooro Kingdom on Wednesday following last month’s death at age 34 of a monarch once known as the “boy king” because of his ascension to the throne as an infant.
articles.body: A news anchor was unexpectedly named the next monarch of Uganda’s Tooro Kingdom on Wednesday following last month’s death at age 34 of a monarch once known as the “boy king” because of his ascension to the throne as an infant. A selection committee for Tooro announced the choice of Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma as crown prince following a search. A cousin of the late king, Kijanangoma is a news anchor and editor with state broadcaster Uganda Broadcasting Corporation. He is likely to be crowned this week to succeed Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who will be buried on Saturday in a funeral expected to be attended by tens of thousands of mourners in a remote city near the Congo border. King Oyo was unmarried at the time of his death from cancer. The event saddened many who had watched him grow from infancy and become a beloved leader for his ancient kingdom. Tooro is one of five traditional kingdoms recognized by Uganda’s government, though they don’t have any formal sovereignty. Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni had asserted that Oyo left a young heir born out of wedlock, but Tooro’s committee looked beyond that in picking Kijanangoma. The choice of Kijanangoma, who is known as a down-to-earth broadcaster, was likely aimed at appealing to traditionalists seeking continuity and those against having another child on the throne. But it could also prove controversial and provoke a legal challenge if Oyo’s devotees feel alienated by the decision. The choice was immediately rejected by his closest relative. “We are just very disappointed,” said Ruth Komuntale, Oyo’s sister, speaking to local broadcaster NBS. “Honestly, to me it’s very dramatic, trying to bring division and turmoil.” She said Oyo’s written will “clearly stated” that he left behind an heir to his throne. Oyo was coronated in 1995 at the age of 3 after his father’s death. He was a curious child in colorful robes and an object of adoration for his hundreds of thousands of subjects. At his coronation, he went through a series of tribal rituals and was led into the royal cemetery to perform the coming-of-age ritual: successfully tossing nine coffee beans into his father’s tomb. Oyo immediately held the unofficial title of the world’s youngest king, a mesmerizing figure even for world leaders introduced to him at national events, including South Africa’s Nelson Mandela. The kid was guided by regents appointed by the kingdom until he became an adult at 18. Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi befriended the Tooro royal family as if they were part of his extended family. Gadhafi made multiple trips to Uganda and supported Oyo and the queen mother for years before his death in October 2011. Uganda’s traditional kingdoms were banned after independence from British colonial rule by a republican president who said he wanted to unify the country, but they were restored in 1993. Although they have no political authority and are legally not allowed to engage in partisan politics, monarchs wield authority as guardians of tribal culture.

articles.title: Former lawyer who pulled gun on ex-wife in Ohio restaurant is convicted of attempted murder
articles.summary: Prosecutors said Matthew Exton tried to carry out the “public execution” of his ex-wife.
articles.body: A former attorney was convicted of attempted murder after officials in Ohio said he tried to carry out the “public execution” of his ex-wife in a Toledo restaurant last year. Matthew Exton, 43, tried to shoot her, but the gun’s safety was on, and a waiter tackled him before he could try again, the Lucas County Prosecutor’s Office said in a news release Friday. Exton was also convicted of two counts of felonious assault, with sentencing enhancements linked to all three charges, the prosecutor’s office said. Exton was acquitted of one count of assault. He is scheduled to be sentenced later this month. During a trial that ended last week, Exton testified that he’d worked as a prosecutor in Michigan and was licensed to practice law in Ohio. He’d handled divorce, family and bankruptcy cases, he said, but he became homeless after he split up with his wife. The couple divorced in 2024, according to court records. He testified that he was frustrated by how she’d handled certain aspects of their divorce when he pulled a Colt Defender on her in the downtown Toledo restaurant on April 11, 2025. Exton saw his ex-wife and her family at the restaurant, which was having its opening night, as he left a different restaurant next door, according to the prosecutor’s office. Exton testified that he pointed the gun to show he was serious about her following a court order. He denied trying to shoot her. “I did not fire,” he said. “I did not hurt her. I did not try to hurt her.” Before he pointed the gun, prosecutors said, Exton ordered a drink and had it taken to the table where his ex was sitting with her family. He spat toward them and left, the prosecutor’s office said. He returned with a gun and headed straight for his ex, according to the release. Video released by the prosecutor’s office showed Exton approaching the table and removing a handgun from his pocket. His ex told authorities that he pointed the gun at her chest and pulled the trigger multiple times, according to a petition for a protection order. “The gun made rapid ‘click’ noises as he pulled the trigger,” she wrote in a statement included in the protection order, which she filed two days after the event. The video showed Exton pointing the Colt as his ex yelled “gun.” The waiter could be seen tackling Exton moments later. Exton tried to fire the weapon, but the safety was still engaged. One round was in the chamber, and seven were in the magazine, the prosecutor’s office said. “Nothing in their training and soft openings at the restaurant could have prepared the staff for what walked through that door,” Lucas County Prosecuting Attorney Julia Bates said in a statement. “The defendant did not come with the intention of having a meal. He came with anger in him and with the intention to commit a public execution of his ex-wife at the restaurant that day.”

articles.title: Tax banks to give some households energy bill cut, unions tell PM
articles.summary: The TUC says a bank surcharge should be reversed - and estimates it would raise £9bn over four years.
articles.body:
The leader of Britain's trade unionists has told Andy Burnham the government should introduce a "social tariff", paid for by a bank surcharge, to help low and middle earners with their energy bills.

A social tariff is a discount on bills based on household income, and the TUC says it believes two-thirds of households could benefit.

The TUC says the bank surcharge, which was reduced in 2023 from 8% to 3% by the then Conservative government, should be reversed - and estimates it would raise £9bn over four years.

TUC leader Paul Nowak said: "I think it will appeal to the prime minister. These are policies that make a difference in the real world and people can see a value in them."

In a wide-ranging BBC interview ahead of its annual congress in Brighton next week, the TUC general secretary said next month's Budget needed to show "the government is back in the service of the British people".

While he said Burnham had got off to a good start as prime minister, he had a series of "asks" of the prime minister and the new Chancellor, John Healey.

Top of his list is more help with energy bills, saying: "We need to drive down inflation – those energy bills are fuelling inflation.

"And millions of families up and down the country are worried about turning on their heating this winter."

Burnham has already offered "breathing space" - as he calls it – on the cost of living by temporarily scrapping VAT on electricity bills from October.

Nowak said the proposal for a social tariff would be popular with Labour MPs; while the Liberal Democrats and the Greens in England and Wales have called for a windfall tax on banks too.

However, UK Finance, which represents well-known banks and lenders, has suggested that heavier levies would undermine the government's ambition to deliver "growth in every postcode" and would damage international competitiveness.

The organisation argues that UK banks face a heavier tax burden than those in the US, for example.

So could the TUC's revenue-raising measure be counter-productive and threaten jobs in finance?

Nowak is sceptical. "I can't believe banks would leave the UK just because we are restoring the surcharge to where it was in 2023. Bank share prices have risen faster here than in New York," he said.

The TUC's demands for tax-raising measures don't stop with the banks, with Nowak arguing the UK has "a tax system that's good at taxing income but not good at capturing wealth".

Nowak suggests a windfall tax on social media companies and for the government to equalise rates of Capital Gains Tax with income tax.

The economist and former minister Lord O'Neill - who has advised Burnham – said recently that wealth taxes were "the last thing that should be happening if we want to see more growth".

Nowak responded: "With respect, I think he is wrong. I'm interested in a growing economy but a growing economy that works for everybody. It is right to ask those with broader shoulders to pay a fairer share."

In addition, Nowak says he doesn't believe the government will deliver on re-industrialisation and on its housing targets without making it easier to borrow to invest.

As Chancellor, Rachel Reeves tweaked her so-called fiscal rules on debt and borrowing but Nowak said he believes the scope this provided for extra investment hasn't been maximised.

"John Healey should leave no stone unturned in allowing us to invest in our economy, in our public services and in our national security," he says.

"He should think about the flexibility he has got within those rules to make investments in the long term."

Don't rule out EU customs union, TUC boss tells Starmer

Nowak has another ask of the government.

The home secretary has announced a change in policy which would see most migrants who are in the UK wait for 10 years rather than the current five before they can settle permanently. Some care workers may have to wait 15 years.

A consultation on the proposed measures closed six months ago, and the government is yet to produce its response.

Nowak – a grandchild of migrants, from Poland and Hong Kong - says: "We should think again not just for care workers but for workers right across the board.

"There are 111,000 staff vacancies in social care at the moment. It's important the rules aren't changed arbitrarily. I would hope and expect this and it needs to be the beginning of a grown-up conversation on immigration."

TUC delegates will debate immigration next week and are likely to echo the call for the government to water down its changes for existing migrants.

Nowak says he felt it was right for Labour to change leaders after disastrous local election results in May, and has been pleased to see a bit of a 'Burnham bounce' in the polls.

And the TUC head warned the prime minister that he needs to provide "meaningful change" if he wants to see off an electoral threat from the populist Right.

He says: "The onus is on Andy Burnham to show he can deliver what he promised.

"If he fails to do it, there are people with glib answers who will turn this country into a more divisive place."

articles.title: Flight carrying Zelenskyy to Norway was delayed in Moldova because of drone incursion
articles.summary: CHISINAU, Moldova — A flight scheduled to carry Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Norway was delayed when authorities closed Moldova’s airspace because of a drone incursion, a government spokesperson said Wednesday.
articles.body: CHISINAU, Moldova — A flight scheduled to carry Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Norway was delayed when authorities closed Moldova’s airspace because of a drone incursion, a government spokesperson said Wednesday. Moldovan police said a Russian drone crashed on Tuesday in a sunflower field on the outskirts of a village in Riscani district, which caused four fires to break out but no injuries. On Wednesday, government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici said Moldova had closed its airspace on Tuesday afternoon to protect aircraft flying over the country at the time, delaying three departures, including the one carrying Zelenskyy. Moldovan authorities confirmed the drone came down and exploded 160 kilometers (100 miles) from Chișinău International Airport. The airspace restrictions were lifted and Zelenskyy’s plane took off later than scheduled. The drone that entered Moldovan airspace on Tuesday crossed into neighboring Romania, a NATO member, where it was tracked through several northeastern counties. The ministry said two F-18 aircraft of the Spanish Air and Space Forces were raised to track its trajectory before it reentered Moldovan airspace. On Wednesday, Moldova’s police said explosives experts discovered fragments of the drone that featured a propulsion system and characteristics similar to a Geran-type drone, which Moscow has used extensively in its full-scale war in Ukraine. “Investigations identified the point of impact, where an explosion occurred and a crater of considerable size was formed,” police said, adding that specialists are continuing investigations “to determine the type and mass of the explosive payload.” Ukraine neighbors both Romania and Moldova, and since Russia’s full invasion in 2022, both countries have reported dozens of drone incidents.
